claim: Drosophila olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) expressing the co-receptor Orco scale their gain inversely with mean odor intensity according to Weber-Fechner's law.
source: We showed previously (Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017) that Drosophila olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) expressing the co-receptor Orco scale their gain inversely with mean odor intensity according to Weber-Fechner's law.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017) that demonstrated this relationship.

claim: Front-end adaptation promotes the reconstruction of odor identity from dynamic odor signals, even in the presence of confounding background odors and rapid intensity fluctuations.
source: Here, we show that this front-end adaptation promotes the reconstruction of odor identity from dynamic odor signals, even in the presence of confounding background odors and rapid intensity fluctuations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the theoretical modeling and computational results presented throughout the manuscript, including compressed sensing decoding accuracy analyses.

claim: Enhancements from front-end adaptation are further aided by known downstream transformations in the antennal lobe and mushroom body.
source: These enhancements are further aided by known downstream transformations in the antennal lobe and mushroom body.
evidence: This claim is supported by the network modeling results shown in Figure 5 and the associated analysis of classification accuracy.

claim: The adaptation mechanism is not intrinsic to the identity of the receptor involved.
source: Our results, which are applicable to various odor classification and reconstruction schemes, stem from the fact that this adaptation mechanism is not intrinsic to the identity of the receptor involved.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental work (Nagel and Wilson, 2011) and is a key assumption in the model.

claim: A feedback mechanism adjusts receptor sensitivity based on the activity of the receptor-Orco complex, according to Weber-Fechner's law.
source: Instead, a feedback mechanism adjusts receptor sensitivity based on the activity of the receptor-Orco complex, according to Weber-Fechner's law.
evidence: This claim is supported by the model equations (Equations 2-3) and citations to experimental work.

claim: A common scaling of the gain across Orco-expressing ORNs may be a key feature of ORN adaptation that helps preserve combinatorial odor codes in naturalistic landscapes.
source: Thus, a common scaling of the gain across Orco-expressing ORNs may be a key feature of ORN adaptation that helps preserve combinatorial odor codes in naturalistic landscapes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational results showing improved odor coding with Weber-Fechner adaptation across multiple decoding schemes.

claim: Individual ORNs typically express a single Or.
source: Individual ORNs, which typically express a single Or, respond to many odorants, while individual odorants activate many distinct ORNs (Friedrich and Korsching, 1997; Hallem and Carlson, 2006; Wang et al., 2010; Nara et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental literature.

claim: Individual ORNs respond to many odorants, while individual odorants activate many distinct ORNs.
source: Individual ORNs, which typically express a single Or, respond to many odorants, while individual odorants activate many distinct ORNs (Friedrich and Korsching, 1997; Hallem and Carlson, 2006; Wang et al., 2010; Nara et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental literature.

claim: Odors are encoded by the combinatorial patterns of activity they elicit in the sensing periphery.
source: Odors are thus encoded by the combinatorial patterns of activity they elicit in the sensing periphery (Malnic et al., 1999; Wang et al., 2010; Hildebrand and Shepherd, 1997; Hallem and Carlson, 2006; de Bruyne et al., 2001; Friedrich and Korsching, 1997), and these patterns are decoded downstream into behavioral response (Wilson, 2013; Davies et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental literature.

claim: Ethologically relevant odors are often mixed with background ones.
source: Still, ethologically relevant odors are often mixed with background ones (Saha et al., 2013; Renou et al., 2015) and intensity can vary widely and rapidly as odors are carried by the wind (Murlis et al., 1992; Weissburg, 2000; Celani et al., 2014; Cardé and Willis, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental and theoretical literature.

claim: Odor intensity can vary widely and rapidly as odors are carried by the wind.
source: Still, ethologically relevant odors are often mixed with background ones (Saha et al., 2013; Renou et al., 2015) and intensity can vary widely and rapidly as odors are carried by the wind (Murlis et al., 1992; Weissburg, 2000; Celani et al., 2014; Cardé and Willis, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental and theoretical literature.

claim: In Drosophila melanogaster, ORN dose response curves exhibit similar Hill coefficients but distinct power-law distributed activation thresholds.
source: In Drosophila melanogaster, ORN dose response curves exhibit similar Hill coefficients but distinct power-law distributed activation thresholds (Hallem and Carlson, 2006; Si et al., 2019), which together with inhibitory odorants enhance coding capacity (Si et al., 2019; Cao et al., 2017; Hallem and Carlson, 2006; Stevens, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental literature.

claim: Power-law distributed activation thresholds together with inhibitory odorants enhance coding capacity.
source: In Drosophila melanogaster, ORN dose response curves exhibit similar Hill coefficients but distinct power-law distributed activation thresholds (Hallem and Carlson, 2006; Si et al., 2019), which together with inhibitory odorants enhance coding capacity (Si et al., 2019; Cao et al., 2017; Hallem and Carlson, 2006; Stevens, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental and theoretical literature.

claim: In antennal lobe glomeruli, mutual lateral inhibition normalizes population response, reducing the dependency of activity patterns on odor concentration.
source: In antennal lobe (AL) glomeruli, mutual lateral inhibition normalizes population response, reducing the dependency of activity patterns on odor concentration (Asahina et al., 2009; Olsen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental literature.

claim: Sparse connectivity to the mushroom body helps maintain neural representations of odors, and facilitates compressed sensing and associative learning schemes.
source: Further downstream, sparse connectivity to the mushroom body (MB) helps maintain neural representations of odors, and facilitates compressed sensing and associative learning schemes (Caron et al., 2013; Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017; Krishnamurthy et al., 2017; Dasgupta et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical and experimental literature.

claim: Temporal features of neural responses contribute to concentration-invariant representations of odor identity.
source: Finally, temporal features of neural responses contribute to concentration-invariant representations of odor identity (Brown et al., 2005; Raman et al., 2010; Gupta and Stopfer, 2014; Wilson et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental literature.

claim: ORN response is initiated upon binding of odorant molecules to olfactory receptors, opening the ion channels they form with the co-receptor Orco.
source: ORN response is initiated upon binding of odorant molecules to olfactory receptors (ORs), opening the ion channels they form with the co-receptor Orco (Larsson et al., 2004; Butterwick et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental literature.

claim: Because of differences in odor-receptor affinities, the responses of ORNs to diverse odorants of the same concentration differ widely.
source: Because of differences in odor-receptor affinities, the responses of ORNs to diverse odorants of the same concentration differ widely (Hallem and Carlson, 2006; Montague et al., 2011; Stensmyr et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental literature.

claim: Downstream from the input nonlinearity, signal transduction and adaptation dynamics exhibit a surprising degree of invariance with respect to odor-receptor identity.
source: In contrast, downstream from this input nonlinearity, signal transduction and adaptation dynamics exhibit a surprising degree of invariance with respect to odor-receptor identity: reverse-correlation analysis of ORN response to fluctuating stimuli produces highly stereotyped, concentration-invariant response filters (Martelli et al., 2013; Si et al., 2019; Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental literature.

claim: Reverse-correlation analysis of ORN response to fluctuating stimuli produces highly stereotyped, concentration-invariant response filters.
source: In contrast, downstream from this input nonlinearity, signal transduction and adaptation dynamics exhibit a surprising degree of invariance with respect to odor-receptor identity: reverse-correlation analysis of ORN response to fluctuating stimuli produces highly stereotyped, concentration-invariant response filters (Martelli et al., 2013; Si et al., 2019; Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental literature.

claim: The invariance in adaptive scaling can be traced back to adaptative feedback mechanisms in odor transduction, upstream of ORN firing.
source: This invariance can be traced back to adaptative feedback mechanisms in odor transduction, upstream of ORN firing (Nagel and Wilson, 2011; Cao et al., 2016; Cafaro, 2016; Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017), which depend on the activity of the signaling pathway rather than on the identity of its receptor (Nagel and Wilson, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental literature.

claim: Adaptive feedback mechanisms depend on the activity of the signaling pathway rather than on the identity of its receptor.
source: This invariance can be traced back to adaptative feedback mechanisms in odor transduction, upstream of ORN firing (Nagel and Wilson, 2011; Cao et al., 2016; Cafaro, 2016; Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017), which depend on the activity of the signaling pathway rather than on the identity of its receptor (Nagel and Wilson, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental literature.

claim: The generality of the adaptive scaling suggests it could be mediated by the highly conserved Orco co-receptor.
source: The generality of the adaptive scaling suggests it could be mediated by the highly conserved Orco co-receptor (Butterwick et al., 2018; Getahun et al., 2013; Getahun et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2017), which has been already been implicated in other types of odor adaptation, taking place over longer timescales (Guo and Smith, 2017; Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is speculative, supported by citations to literature on Orco and its role in adaptation.

claim: Orco has been implicated in other types of odor adaptation, taking place over longer timescales.
source: The generality of the adaptive scaling suggests it could be mediated by the highly conserved Orco co-receptor (Butterwick et al., 2018; Getahun et al., 2013; Getahun et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2017), which has been already been implicated in other types of odor adaptation, taking place over longer timescales (Guo and Smith, 2017; Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental literature.

claim: In E. coli chemotaxis, adaptive feedback via the Weber-Fechner Law robustly maintains sensitivity over concentration changes.
source: While in a simpler system such as E. coli chemotaxis (Waite et al., 2018), adaptive feedback via the Weber-Fechner Law robustly maintains sensitivity over concentration changes, the implication for a multiple-channel system – which combines information from hundreds of cells with overlapping receptive fields – is less clear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on E. coli chemotaxis.

claim: Front-end adaptive mechanism promotes the accurate discrimination of odor signals from backgrounds of varying molecular complexity.
source: We find that this front-end adaptive mechanism promotes the accurate discrimination of odor signals from backgrounds of varying molecular complexity, and aids other known mechanisms of neural processing in the olfactory circuit to maintain representations of odor identity across environmental changes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational results presented in Figures 2-5.

claim: The model reproduces the essential features of ORN response to odorant pulses.
source: This minimal model reproduces the essential features of ORN response to odorant pulses (Nagel and Wilson, 2011; Martelli et al., 2013; Cao et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental literature and by the model results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The diversity of temporal firing responses and tuning curves measured experimentally arise naturally in the model due to the distribution of chemical affinity constants and the nonlinearity of Equation 2.
source: The diversity of temporal firing responses and tuning curves measured experimentally (Hallem and Carlson, 2006; Montague et al., 2011; Brown et al., 2005; Gupta and Stopfer, 2014; Raman et al., 2010) arise naturally in the model due to the distribution of chemical affinity constants and the nonlinearity of Equation 2 (Figure 1B-Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental literature and demonstrated in Figures 1B-1E.

claim: This process adjusts the sensitivity of the ORN by matching the dose responses to the mean signal concentration, while maintaining their log-slopes.
source: This process adjusts the sensitivity of the ORN by matching the dose responses to the mean signal concentration, while maintaining their log-slopes (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is demonstrated in Figure 1F showing dose-response curves before and after adaptation.

claim: For foreground odors mixed with background odors to which the system has adapted, the dose response curves exhibit background-dependent shifts.
source: However, for foreground odors mixed with background odors to which the system has adapted, the dose response curves now exhibit background-dependent shifts (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is demonstrated in Figure 1G showing dose-response curves for different background conditions.

claim: Responses across different odor intensities are well separated by odor identity in the adaptive system, but less so in the non-adaptive system.
source: Similarly, responses across different odor intensities are well separated by odor identity in the adaptive system, but less so in the non-adaptive system (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is demonstrated in Figure 2C showing t-SNE clustering across intensities.

claim: The adaptive system retains coding capacity as it confronts novel odors.
source: Calculating the mutual information between odor and ORN response in time shows that the adaptive system retains coding capacity as it confronts novel odors (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), whereas the non-adaptive system maintains coding capacity in a far more limited range of odor concentration.
evidence: This claim is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 showing mutual information over time.

claim: This initial effect increases odor coding performance, as the firing rates can distribute more broadly across the dynamical range of the ORNs, before adaptation is effected.
source: This initial effect increases odor coding performance, as the firing rates can distribute more broadly across the dynamical range of the ORNs, before adaptation is effected (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is explained by the analysis and demonstrated in Figure 2E.

claim: Naturally occurring odors are sparse, typically comprised of only a few odorants.
source: However, naturally occurring odors are sparse, typically comprised of only a few odorants.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about natural odors.

claim: The decoding of sufficiently sparse signals from lower dimensional responses is rigorously guaranteed by the theory of compressed sensing.
source: Indeed, the decoding of sufficiently sparse signals from lower dimensional responses is rigorously guaranteed by the theory of compressed sensing (CS) (Donoho, 2006; Candès et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational compressed sensing literature.

claim: Without adaptation, accuracy is maintained within the range of receptor sensitivity for monomolecular backgrounds but is virtually eliminated as background complexity rises.
source: Without adaptation, accuracy is maintained within the range of receptor sensitivity for monomolecular backgrounds but is virtually eliminated as background complexity rises (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is demonstrated in Figure 3B showing decoding accuracy for the non-adaptive system.

claim: The range of sensitivity is broader in the adaptive system and is substantially more robust across odor concentration and complexity.
source: The range of sensitivity is broader in the adaptive system and is substantially more robust across odor concentration and complexity (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is demonstrated in Figure 3C showing decoding accuracy for the adaptive system.

claim: Without ORN adaptation, sufficiently strong backgrounds eliminate the ability to reconstruct the identity of individual odor whiffs, irrespective of the complexity of either the foreground or background odor.
source: Without ORN adaptation, sufficiently strong backgrounds eliminate the ability to reconstruct the identity of individual odor whiffs, irrespective of the complexity of either the foreground or background odor (Figure 3E, blue lines).
evidence: This claim is demonstrated in Figure 3E showing decoding accuracy for naturalistic signals without adaptation.

claim: For simple odors, a limited set of earliest responding neurons fully accounts for the odor identity.
source: For simple odors, a limited set of earliest responding neurons fully accounts for the odor identity (Figure 4A), in agreement with primacy coding.
evidence: This claim is demonstrated in Figure 4A showing decoding accuracy as a function of active ORNs.

claim: As expected for more complex odor mixtures, the full repertoire is required for accurate decoding.
source: As expected for more complex odor mixtures, the full repertoire is required for accurate decoding.
evidence: This claim is demonstrated in Figure 4A showing that more ORNs are needed for complex odors.

claim: Primacy coding predicts that for stronger stimuli, responses occur earlier, since the primacy set is realized quicker.
source: Primacy coding also predicts that for stronger stimuli, responses occur earlier, since the primacy set is realized quicker, which our framework replicates (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is demonstrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: With adaptation, primacy sets are highly consistent across background confounds for all but the smallest primacy orders.
source: We compared the primacy sets of odor A for 1000 different choices of odor B, finding that, with adaptation, primacy sets are highly consistent across background confounds for all but the smallest primacy orders (Figure 4B-Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is demonstrated in Figures 4B and 4C showing primacy set consistency.

claim: Primacy set consistency holds true for backgrounds of different concentrations.
source: This also holds true for backgrounds of different concentrations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting a central role for front-end adaptation in reinforcing primacy codes across differing environmental conditions.
evidence: This claim is demonstrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Removing ORN adaption while maintaining divisive normalization substantially reduces accuracy (down to 65% for 1000 odor identities).
source: Removing ORN adaption while maintaining divisive normalization substantially reduces accuracy (down to 65% for 1000 odor identities).
evidence: This claim is demonstrated in Figure 5A showing classification accuracy without ORN adaptation.

claim: These results strongly implicate front-end adaptation as a key player in maintaining odor identity representations, before signals are further processed downstream.
source: These results strongly implicate front-end adaptation as a key player in maintaining odor identity representations, before signals are further processed downstream.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the classification results shown in Figure 5.

claim: When acting alone, either divisive normalization or ORN adaptation can help with valence classification, although the effect of ORN adaptation is slightly stronger.
source: When acting alone, either divisive normalization or ORN adaptation can help, although the effect of ORN adaptation is slightly stronger.
evidence: This claim is demonstrated in Figure 5B showing valence classification accuracy.

claim: When both divisive normalization and ORN adaptation are active, valence classification accuracy improves further.
source: When both are active, accuracy improves further, suggesting that these distinct adaptive transformations may act jointly at different stages of neural processing in preserving representations of odor identity.
evidence: This claim is demonstrated in Figure 5B and represents an inference about the joint action of these mechanisms.

claim: Weber-Law adaptation at the very front-end of the insect olfactory circuit may contribute significantly to the preservation of neural representations of odor identity amid confounding odors and intensity fluctuations.
source: Weber-Law adaptation at the very front-end of the insect olfactory circuit (Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017; Cafaro, 2016; Cao et al., 2016) may contribute significantly to the preservation of neural representations of odor identity amid confounding odors and intensity fluctuations.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the computational results presented.

claim: This mechanism of dynamic adaptation confers significant benefits in coding fidelity, without the need for ORN-specific parameterizations.
source: Drawing on experimental evidence for a number of ORN-invariant response features (Nagel and Wilson, 2011; Martelli et al., 2013; Stevens, 2016; Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017; Si et al., 2019), we have found that this mechanism of dynamic adaptation confers significant benefits in coding fidelity, without the need for ORN-specific parameterizations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results and supported by citations to experimental literature.

claim: A slight breaking of Weber scaling may aid combinatorial coding, by spreading firing rates more fully over the ORN dynamic range, while still preventing saturation.
source: Our results also suggest that a slight breaking of Weber scaling may aid combinatorial coding, by spreading firing rates more fully over the ORN dynamic range, while still preventing saturation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: Small deviations from the strict Weber-Fechner scaling have been observed.
source: Such small deviations from the strict Weber-Fechner scaling have been observed (see extended figures in Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental observations.

claim: The framework incorporates many observed features of the Drosophila olfactory system.
source: While our framework incorporates many observed features of the Drosphila olfactory system – Weber-Law adaptation, power-law distributed receptor affinities, temporal filter invariance, connectivity topologies – it is minimal.
evidence: This is a statement about the model design and its relationship to experimental observations.

claim: The model is minimal and does not include all features of the olfactory system.
source: While our framework incorporates many observed features of the Drosphila olfactory system – Weber-Law adaptation, power-law distributed receptor affinities, temporal filter invariance, connectivity topologies – it is minimal. We considered only one of the chemoreceptor families expressed in the fly antenna (Joseph and Carlson, 2015) and ignored possible contributions of odor binding proteins (Vogt and Riddiford, 1981; Menuz et al., 2014), inhibitory odorants (Cao et al., 2017), and odorant-odorant antagonism (Reddy et al., 2018), which could further boost coding capacity and preserve representation sparsity.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the model.

claim: Lateral inhibition between glomeruli helps tame saturation and boost weak signals.
source: Lateral inhibition between glomeruli helps tame saturation and boost weak signals (Olsen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental literature.

claim: The sparse degree of connectivity to either the olfactory bulb (vertebrates) or mushroom body (insects) may be precisely tuned to optimize the capacity to learn associations.
source: The sparse degree of connectivity to either the olfactory bulb (vertebrates) or mushroom body (insects) may also be precisely tuned to optimize the capacity to learn associations (Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to theoretical literature.

claim: Some downstream features act in concert with front-end dynamic adaptation in maintaining representations of odor identity.
source: In this work, we find that some of these downstream features act in concert with front-end dynamic adaptation in maintaining representations of odor identity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the network modeling results in Figure 5.

claim: The unique temporal patterns of neural response have been implicated as signatures of odor identity.
source: Other studies have implicated the unique temporal patterns of neural response as signatures of odor identity (Raman et al., 2010; Gupta and Stopfer, 2011; Brown et al., 2005; Gupta and Stopfer, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental literature.

claim: ORN and projection neuron time traces form distinct trajectories in low-dimensional projections, and cluster by odor identity.
source: ORN and projection neuron time traces form distinct trajectories in low-dimensional projections, and cluster by odor identity, much as we have found here for static responses at different concentrations (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim connects the current results to prior experimental findings and is demonstrated in Figure 2.

claim: In locusts PNs, the trajectories elicited by foreground odors when presented in distinct backgrounds exhibit some degree of overlap.
source: In locusts PNs, the trajectories elicited by foreground odors when presented in distinct backgrounds exhibit some degree of overlap; although partial, these overlaps were nonetheless sufficient to maintain background-invariant decoding from Kenyon cell responses (Saha et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental literature.

claim: It was suggested that background filtering likely occurs at the level of ORNs themselves.
source: It was therefore suggested that background filtering likely occurs at the level of ORNs themselves (Saha et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental literature.

claim: In the framework, temporal coding is implicit: because the input nonlinearity depends on the diversity of binding affinities, odor signals are naturally formatted into temporal patterns that are both odor- and ORN-specific.
source: Likewise, in our framework, temporal coding is implicit: because the input nonlinearity depends on the diversity of binding affinities, odor signals are naturally formatted into temporal patterns that are both odor- and ORN-specific (Figure 1D-Figure 1E).
evidence: This is an explanation of how temporal coding emerges in the model, demonstrated in Figures 1D-1E.

claim: Front-end adaptation enhances the robustness of other combinatorial coding schemes, such as primacy coding.
source: Moreover, we find that front-end adaptation enhances the robustness of other combinatorial coding schemes, such as primacy coding (Wilson et al., 2017), which relies on the temporal order of ORN activation but not absolute firing rate (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the primacy coding results shown in Figure 4.

claim: In bacterial chemotaxis, Weber Law adaptation is enacted through a feedback loop from the output activity of the receptor-kinase complexes onto the enzymes modifying receptor sensitivity.
source: In the well-characterized chemosensory system of bacterial chemotaxis, Weber Law adaptation is enacted through a feedback loop from the output activity of the receptor-kinase complexes onto the enzymes modifying receptor sensitivity (Waite et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on bacterial chemotaxis.

claim: It has been shown that transduction activity feeds back onto the sensitivity of Or-Orco ligand-gated cation channels, enabling the Weber-Fechner relation.
source: It is interesting that some aspects of this logic are also present in ORNs: although the molecular players are different (and still largely unknown, although likely involving calcium channel signaling, Cao et al., 2016), it has been shown that transduction activity feeds back onto the sensitivity of Or-Orco ligand-gated cation channels, enabling the Weber-Fechner relation (Nagel and Wilson, 2011; Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017; Cao et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental literature.

claim: The adaptation mechanism appears to act similarly across ORNs.
source: That this adaptation mechanism appears to act similarly across ORNs (Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017; Martelli et al., 2013; Cao et al., 2016) suggests the possible involvement of the universal co-receptor Orco, whose role in long-term adaptation has recently been reported (Getahun et al., 2013; Getahun et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental literature and represents a speculative inference.

claim: The identification of four subunits comprising the Orco-Or ion channel suggest that generic Or/Orco complexes may contain multiple odorant binding sites.
source: Further, the identification of four subunits comprising the Orco-Or ion channel suggest that generic Or/Orco complexes may contain multiple odorant binding sites, which when included in our model supports our general findings (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural knowledge and modeling results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Weber Law ensures that sensory systems remain in the regime of maximum sensitivity, broadening dynamic range and maintaining information capacity.
source: Weber Law ensures that sensory systems remain in the regime of maximum sensitivity, broadening dynamic range and maintaining information capacity (Wark et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to theoretical literature.

claim: For a single-channel system, maintaining maximum sensitivity requires matching the midpoint of the dose-response curve to the mean ligand concentration.
source: For a single-channel system, this requires matching the midpoint of the dose-response curve to the mean ligand concentration (Nemenman, 2012), a strategy which may fail in multi-channel systems with overlapping tuning curves: adaptation to one signal could inhibit identification of others, if the signals excite some but not all the same sensors, as in Figure 1G.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to theoretical literature and illustrated in Figure 1G.

claim: The Weber-Fechner scaling increases the likelihood that the restricted isometry property is satisfied, beyond that in the non-adaptive system.
source: Indeed, the Weber-Fechner scaling increases the likelihood that this property is satisfied, beyond that in the non-adaptive system (SI text and Figure 3—figure supplement 4 - Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Restricted isometry does not require that response repertoires are invariant to environmental changes.
source: Still, restricted isometry does not require that response repertoires are invariant to environmental changes. That is, even if the subset of active ORNs were concentration-dependent, odors could still in principle be fully reconstructible by CS.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the requirements of compressed sensing.

claim: Some signature of response invariance emerges as a natural byproduct of front-end adaptation.
source: Nonetheless, our results in t-SNE clustering (Figure 2), primacy coding (Figure 4B–4C), and odor classification (Figure 5) suggest that some signature of response invariance emerges as a natural byproduct of front-end adaptation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple analyses shown in Figures 2, 4, and 5.

claim: Weber Law adaptation can play an integral part in maintaining combinatorial codes amid changing environmental conditions.
source: Together, this implies that Weber Law adaptation, whether required by the olfactory circuit for precise signal reconstruction (as in CS) or for developing odor associations (as in classification), can play an integral part in maintaining combinatorial codes amid changing environmental conditions.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, synthesizing all the results presented.
